analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 25% tax on big oil companies' windfall profits and spends the money on highways.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the bill, which would have taxed oil companies' excess profits at 25% in 2008 and 2009 and directed the money to the Highway Trust Fund.
analysis.plain_summary: When oil prices were driving record profits in 2008, this bill would have charged large oil companies a 25% tax on profits above their normal 2003–2007 level (plus 10%). Only companies with over $1 billion in gross receipts would pay. The money would go into the Highway Trust Fund, which pays for road and transit projects. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Highway and transit users, since the tax revenue would flow into the Highway Trust Fund [S2][S3]. More broadly, anyone paying at the gas pump in 2008, who would see a share of record oil-company profits recycled into public infrastructure rather than kept by the companies.

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposed a 25% excise tax on the 'windfall profit' of large oil companies for 2008 and 2009 — the amount their income exceeded their average 2003–2007 profit plus 10%. [S2][S3]
It applied to integrated oil companies and any other crude oil producer or refiner with over $1 billion in gross receipts, so only the largest firms would pay. [S3]
All revenue from the tax would be transferred to the Highway Trust Fund, the fund that finances federal road and transit spending. [S2][S3]
The tax was temporary, applying only to tax years beginning in 2008 and 2009. [S2][S3]

analysis.who_pays: Large oil companies — integrated majors and any producer or refiner of crude oil with over $1 billion in gross receipts — would pay 25% of their excess profits. To the extent companies passed the cost along, drivers could pay somewhat higher gasoline prices, though the tax applied only to profits above a normal baseline. [S3]

drawbacks.text: A windfall profits tax can be shifted to consumers through higher prices, so drivers might have paid part of it at the pump. [S3]
The bill allowed companies to deduct the windfall tax payment from their income taxes, which reduced the net revenue raised. [S3]
Taxes on excess profits can discourage investment in domestic production and refining, which could tighten supply over time — a standard objection to this kind of tax. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a narrow, temporary tax at the largest oil companies during a period of record profits and directed the money to a widely used public purpose. Its main honest costs are the risk of some price pass-through to drivers, the deductibility that shrinks the take, and possible dampening of investment. On balance the design is defensible, though imperfect.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Charles Schumer introduced the bill on March 13, 2008, during a period of high oil and gasoline prices. [S1][S5]
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance. [S5]
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the bill expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009. [S1][S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large oil companies came out ahead: they kept profits above the normal baseline untaxed, and the Highway Trust Fund never received the new revenue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large oil companies and their shareholders

for.name: Charles E. Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded its referral to the Senate Finance Committee.

against.name: Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing or markup; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.role: Industry subject to the windfall profits tax
against.what_they_did: Opposed windfall profits tax proposals during the 2008 oil price spike, as the tax would have directly reduced their earnings.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call record exists; the sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican support is recorded. [S4]

industries.industry: Large oil companies (integrated majors and big producers/refiners)
industries.note: The bill would have taken 25% of their profits above a normal baseline for 2008–2009 and routed it to highway funding. Because the bill died in committee, the industry kept those profits, and the cost of that outcome falls on road and transit users who would have benefited from the revenue. [S3]
